title: Sir Garry Sobers, Cricket's Greatest All-Rounder, Dies at 89 as India and England Pay Tribute at Lord's
excerpt: The Barbadian legend who scored 8,032 Test runs, took 235 wickets and hit the first-ever six sixes in an over died peacefully at his home in Barbados, 10 days before his 90th birthday.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Sir Garfield Sobers, cricket's greatest all-rounder, passed away at 89 in Barbados.
  • He scored 8,032 Test runs and took 235 wickets in a 20-year career.
  • Sobers set the record for highest Test innings with 365 not out in 1958.
  • England players wore black armbands at Lord's to honor Sobers during an ODI.
  • He was knighted in 1975 and is a symbol of Caribbean excellence.
  • Sir Garfield "Garry" Sobers, widely regarded as cricket's greatest all-rounder, died on Friday, July 17, at his home in Barbados at the age of 89
  • He scored 8,032 runs at an average of 57.78 in 93 Tests, took 235 wickets, and held 109 catches across a 20-year international career
  • Sobers set the record for the highest individual Test innings — 365 not out against Pakistan in 1958 — and hit the first-ever six sixes in an over in first-class cricket
  • England players wore black armbands during the series-deciding ODI against India at Lord's in tribute to the legendary Barbadian

The End of a Great Innings

Sir Garfield "Garry" Sobers, the man many consider the finest cricketer to ever walk onto a field, died on Friday at his home in Highgate Gardens, St. Michael, Barbados. He was 89, just 10 days short of his 90th birthday. His son Daniel confirmed the death was from age-related causes.

Cricket West Indies broke the news with a simple statement: "A great innings has come to an end. In our hearts, now and forever, Sir Garfield Sobers."

https://x.com/ianuragthakur/status/2078421492149424134

Born on July 28, 1936, in Bridgetown as the fifth of six children, Sobers lost his father — a seaman in the Canadian merchant navy — when German forces sank his ship during World War II. Garfield was five years old. Raised by his mother Thelma, he first played cricket in the roads and on the beaches of Barbados, fashioning bats from fence posts and balls from lumps of tar.

Records That May Never Be Matched

Sobers made his first-class debut for Barbados at 16 and was playing Test cricket for the West Indies by 17. In a career spanning 93 Tests from 1954 to 1974, he compiled 8,032 runs at an average of 57.78 — the fourth-highest in Test history among batters with more than 5,000 runs — including 26 centuries. He also took 235 wickets at 34.03 and held 109 catches, most of them in close-catching positions where reflexes matter more than range.

His 365 not out against Pakistan in 1958 stood as the highest individual Test innings for 36 years until fellow West Indian Brian Lara surpassed it in 1994. In 1968, playing for Nottinghamshire against Glamorgan, he became the first cricketer to hit six sixes in a single over — a feat that entered sporting folklore.

What set Sobers apart was not just quantity but range. He could bowl left-arm fast-medium with the new ball, switch to orthodox spin, and then deliver wrist spin. Don Bradman, after watching Sobers score 254 for a World XI in Melbourne in 1971-72, called it the best innings he had ever seen on Australian soil.

"Ian Chappell once told me, 'Mikey, this talk about Garry being the best all-rounder there is, he's the best batsman I've seen.' He singled him out as a batsman as well."

— Michael Holding, West Indies fast bowling legend

Indian Legends Remember a Rival and an Idol

The tributes from India were particularly poignant. Sunil Gavaskar, whose debut Test series in 1970-71 came against a Sobers-captained West Indies, called him "the greatest of them all."

"For anyone who loves this beautiful game, Sir Garry wasn't just a cricketer; he was the ultimate standard of what a cricketer could be," Gavaskar wrote on X. "He was a master of five. He could bat like a dream, bowl fast-medium with the new ball, switch seamlessly to orthodox left-arm spin, bowl wrist spin, and field like a panther."

Virat Kohli posted that "cricket has lost one of its greatest," while VVS Laxman described Sobers as a "true giant of the game." Madan Lal, who won the 1983 World Cup, said simply: "Such an all-rounder has never been born, nor will there ever be another."

Black Armbands at Lord's

At Lord's, the home of cricket, England paid tribute during the series-deciding ODI against India on Sunday. Players wore black armbands in Sobers's memory. England all-rounder Jacob Bethell, who grew up in Barbados and knew Sobers personally, revealed that the legend had written him a reference to help secure a sports scholarship to Rugby School in Birmingham — a gesture that helped launch his international career.

"He had a presence about him," Bethell told reporters. "Every time he walked into anywhere, the place would just come alive. It was unbelievable to spend a bit of time with him and be around someone of that calibre."

Legacy Beyond the Boundary

Cricket West Indies President Kishore Shallow said Sobers represented far more than sporting excellence. "He became a symbol of Caribbean excellence, resilience and hope during a defining period in the region's history."

The ICC's top individual honour, the Sir Garfield Sobers Trophy, awarded annually to the world's best men's international cricketer, will carry his name into perpetuity. He was knighted in 1975, held National Hero status in Barbados, and was named one of Wisden's Cricketers of the Century.

Michael Holding captured it best: "There aren't enough words that can be written or said to fully give the great man justice. Every West Indian cricketer would have and should continue to walk proudly knowing the best ever came from the same place they're from."
